subject: math
description: Students apply the product, quotient, and power rules for logarithms (together with the change-of-base formula and the identities $\log_b b = 1$, $\log_b 1 = 0$, $b^{\log_b x} = x$, and $\log_b b^x = x$) to expand a single logarithm into a sum or difference of logarithms and to condense a sum or difference into a single logarithm. They then solve exponential equations by taking logarithms of both sides and solve logarithmic equations by condensing to a single log and rewriting in exponential form. For every logarithmic equation they must verify each candidate solution against the domain requirement that the argument of every logarithm be positive, and discard any extraneous solutions.
subSkills: Expand a single logarithm using the product rule $\log_b(MN)=\log_b M+\log_b N$
Expand using the quotient rule $\log_b\left(\frac{M}{N}\right)=\log_b M-\log_b N$
Expand using the power rule $\log_b(M^p)=p\log_b M$, including roots written as fractional exponents
Condense a sum or difference of logarithms back into a single logarithm with coefficient 1
Apply the change-of-base formula $\log_b a=\frac{\log a}{\log b}=\frac{\ln a}{\ln b}$ to evaluate or rewrite
Use logarithm identities $\log_b b=1$, $\log_b 1=0$, $b^{\log_b x}=x$, $\log_b b^x=x$
Solve exponential equations of the form $b^{f(x)}=c$ by taking a logarithm of both sides
Solve logarithmic equations by condensing to one log and rewriting in exponential form
Determine the domain of each logarithmic expression (argument $>0$) and check candidate solutions for extraneous roots

problemArchetypes.name: Expand a logarithm
problemArchetypes.example: Expand $\log_2\left(\frac{x^3\sqrt{y}}{z}\right)$ as a sum and difference of logarithms with no products, quotients, or exponents inside any log. Answer: $3\log_2 x+\frac{1}{2}\log_2 y-\log_2 z$.

problemArchetypes.name: Condense to a single logarithm
problemArchetypes.example: Write $2\ln x+\frac{1}{3}\ln y-\ln 5$ as a single logarithm. Answer: $\ln\left(\frac{x^2\sqrt[3]{y}}{5}\right)$.

problemArchetypes.name: Evaluate using properties or change of base
Solve with condensing and an extraneous root
problemArchetypes.example: Solve $\log_3 x+\log_3(x-2)=1$. Condense: $\log_3\big(x(x-2)\big)=1\Rightarrow x^2-2x-3=0\Rightarrow x=3$ or $x=-1$. Reject $x=-1$ (makes $\log_3 x$ undefined); answer $x=3$.

Easy.description: A single property applied once, or a one-step equation. Expand or condense an expression that needs exactly one rule (product, quotient, or power). Solve $b^x=c$ where $c$ is an exact power of $b$, or solve a single-log equation with no extraneous-root risk.
constraints: At most one logarithm rule is needed, applied a single time
Exponential equations have an exact integer or simple rational answer, e.g. $2^x=32\Rightarrow x=5$
Logarithmic equations contain exactly one log term and yield one valid solution
No quadratic arises; no candidate solution needs to be rejected

Medium.description: Two or three properties combined. Expand or condense expressions mixing products, quotients, and powers (including a square root as a $\frac{1}{2}$ power). Solve exponential equations requiring a logarithm and change of base, or logarithmic equations that require condensing two log terms before rewriting in exponential form.
constraints: Combines two or three rules in one expansion or condensation
Exponential answers are exact logarithms, e.g. $x=\frac{\ln 20}{\ln 3}-1$, not clean integers
Logarithmic equations require condensing two terms, then rewriting $\log_b A=k$ as $A=b^k$
At most one candidate solution may need an extraneous-root check

Hard.description: Multi-step problems whose algebra produces a quadratic (or a substitution) and require an explicit domain analysis. Solving forces condensing, rewriting, solving a quadratic in $x$ or in $u=b^x$, then testing every candidate against the positivity of all arguments and discarding extraneous solutions, or proving none exist.
constraints: Condensing yields a quadratic argument, e.g. $\log_b x+\log_b(x-c)=k$
Exponential equations may be quadratic in form, e.g. $e^{2x}-5e^{x}+6=0$ solved by substitution $u=e^x$
Student must state the domain (every argument $>0$) and reject at least one candidate, or justify that a solution set is empty
Answers are exact (radicals, $\ln$, $\log$, fractions); approximations only if the problem asks for one

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Treats the log of a sum as the sum of logs
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Writes $\log_b(M+N)=\log_b M+\log_b N$, so expands $\log_2(x+8)$ as $\log_2 x+\log_2 8$ instead of leaving it unchanged

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Misapplies the quotient rule as a quotient of logs
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Writes $\log_b\left(\frac{M}{N}\right)=\frac{\log_b M}{\log_b N}$ instead of $\log_b M-\log_b N$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Drops the power-rule coefficient or applies it to the wrong factor
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Expands $\log_2(x^3 y)$ as $\log_2 x+3\log_2 y$ or $\log_2 x^3+\log_2 y$ instead of $3\log_2 x+\log_2 y$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Forgets a root is a fractional exponent when expanding
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Expands $\log_b\sqrt{y}$ as $\log_b y$ instead of $\frac{1}{2}\log_b y$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: When condensing, adds coefficients into the log as multipliers instead of exponents
Cancels or simplifies $\log_b b^x$ incorrectly, treating $\log$ as a multiplier
Solves an exponential equation by dividing out the base instead of taking a logarithm
Rewrites $\log_b A=k$ in exponential form with base and exponent swapped
commonMisconceptions.distractor: From $\log_4(2x-1)=2$ writes $2x-1=2^4=16$... uses base 2 instead, giving $2x-1=4^2$ mishandled, e.g. solving $2x-1=2^4$ or $2x-1=4\cdot 2$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Accepts a negative or out-of-domain candidate as a valid solution
commonMisconceptions.distractor: From $\log_3 x+\log_3(x-2)=1$ keeps both $x=3$ and $x=-1$ instead of rejecting $x=-1$, which makes the arguments negative

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Rejects a valid solution by misjudging the domain
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Discards a legitimate solution because one intermediate factor is negative, even though every actual logarithm argument is positive at that value
